title: SQL Server and Azure SQL index architecture and design guide
organization_author: Microsoft (SQL Server documentation; author adbadram, reviewers dfurman/derekw)
subcategory: Indexes, clustered key / primary key design, physical table storage, partitioning
core_concepts: clustered index stores all rows (B+ tree) vs heap
desirable clustered key properties: narrow, unique, ever-increasing, immutable, not nullable
primary key is clustered by default but can be made nonclustered
nonclustered index design: SARGable key columns, INCLUDE columns, covering indexes, filtered indexes
hard limits: 16 key columns / 900 bytes key, 1,023 included columns
OLTP = few narrow rowstore indexes; OLAP = clustered columnstore
table partitioning: partition function/scheme, 15,000 partitions, aligned indexes
engineering_principles: RECOMMENDED (all workloads, strongest OLTP): 'With a few exceptions, every table should have a clustered index'; a heap 'is generally not recommended'. The clustered key is embedded in every nonclustered index, so it should be narrow, unique, ever-increasing (avoids page splits), immutable and non-nullable; 'a clustered index key with a single int or bigint not nullable column has all of these properties if it's populated by an IDENTITY clause or a ... sequence', whereas a uniqueidentifier key 'is wider ... and doesn't satisfy the ever-increasing property unless the values are generated sequentially'. If the PK does not satisfy these properties 'create the constraint as nonclustered and create a different clustered index instead'. 'Avoid over-indexing heavily updated tables and keep indexes narrow'; modify an existing index rather than add near-duplicates; put only predicate/sort/aggregate columns in the key and cover the rest with INCLUDE. MANDATORY: key size and column-count limits; LOB/json/vector columns cannot be key columns. Partitioning page (same doc set): 'partitioning rarely improves performance in OLTP systems'; 'Avoid designs with the number of partitions in many hundreds or thousands unless strictly necessary'; clustered key must contain the partitioning column.
practical_examples: CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Address_PostalCode ON Person.Address (PostalCode) INCLUDE (AddressLine1, AddressLine2, City, StateProvinceID) -- covering index example from the guide; partitioning page example: CREATE PARTITION FUNCTION [myDateRangePF1](DATETIME) AS RANGE RIGHT FOR VALUES ('2022-02-01', '2022-03-01', ...); guidance to set ALTER TABLE ... LOCK_ESCALATION = AUTO for partition-level escalation.
why_it_matters: This is Microsoft's authoritative statement of why SQL Server tables need surrogate, monotonically increasing clustered keys and why GUID clustered keys are discouraged; it directly drives primary-key and index decisions in any SQL Server schema and gives the OLTP-vs-OLAP index split (rowstore vs columnstore).
authority_rationale: Official vendor documentation maintained by the SQL Server product group; page shows ms.date and applies-to versions (SQL Server 2017-2025, Azure SQL Database/MI, Fabric SQL database).
notes: Also read: Partitioned tables and indexes, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/partitions/partitioned-tables-and-indexes (ms.date 2025-12-29; 15,000-partition limit; RANGE LEFT default; single filegroup recommended unless tiered storage/piecemeal restore). Default moniker on both pages is sql-server-ver17 (SQL Server 2025).

title: Primary and foreign key constraints (SQL Server)
subcategory: Keys, constraints, referential integrity, identifiers, schemas
core_concepts: one primary key per table, max 32 columns / 900 bytes, columns forced NOT NULL
PK index is clustered by default if no clustered index exists
foreign keys do not auto-create an index
cascading referential actions NO ACTION / CASCADE / SET NULL / SET DEFAULT
253 outgoing FK references; 10,000 incoming (DELETE only)
UNIQUE allows one NULL and creates a nonclustered unique index by default
CHECK constraints pass UNKNOWN (NULL) and are not validated on DELETE
identifier rules (1-128 characters) and schema-as-namespace
engineering_principles: MANDATORY engine rules: single PK, 900-byte/32-column PK limit, PK columns not null, 999 nonclustered + 1 clustered index cap, 253 outgoing FK references. RECOMMENDED: 'manually creating an index on a foreign key is often useful' for joins and PK-change checks, but 'creating this index isn't required'. CHECK: 'Because null values evaluate to UNKNOWN, their presence in expressions might override a constraint'; 'Avoid data type conversion in constraint definitions' (breaks partition SWITCH). Identifiers: 'Both regular and delimited identifiers must contain from 1 through 128 characters'; avoid '#'/'##' prefixes on non-temp objects and '@@' names; delimit reserved words. Schemas: 'A schema is a named container for database objects'; permissions granted on a schema 'are automatically applied as new objects are added'; do not use the legacy db_* schemas for user objects.
practical_examples: CREATE TABLE TableX (KeyCol INT PRIMARY KEY, Description NVARCHAR(80)); -- unnamed PK gets system name PK__TableX__...; CONSTRAINT [PK_SalesOrderDetail_Order_SalesOrderDetailID] PRIMARY KEY CLUSTERED ([Order] ASC, [SalesOrderDetailID] ASC); CHECK (salary >= 15000 AND salary <= 100000); four-part naming Server.Database.DatabaseSchema.DatabaseObject.
why_it_matters: Defines the integrity toolkit (PK/FK/UNIQUE/CHECK) and its SQL Server-specific traps (FK indexes not automatic, NULL semantics in CHECK, cascading restrictions with triggers/timestamp) plus naming/namespace rules every SQL Server schema must obey.
authority_rationale: Official vendor documentation with explicit ms.date and applies-to (SQL Server 2016+, Azure SQL DB/MI, Fabric SQL database).
notes: Companion pages read: Unique constraints and check constraints, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/tables/unique-constraints-and-check-constraints (ms.date 2023-12-29); Database identifiers, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/databases/database-identifiers (ms.date 2026-04-08); Ownership and user-schema separation, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/security/authentication-access/ownership-and-user-schema-separation (ms.date 2024-05-09). No official naming-convention (case/prefix) guidance exists on these pages, only identifier rules.

title: money and smallmoney (Transact-SQL) and related T-SQL data type references (decimal, datetime, datetime2, nchar/nvarchar, uniqueidentifier, NEWSEQUENTIALID)
organization_author: Microsoft (SQL Server T-SQL reference; author uc-msft)
core_concepts: money/smallmoney: 4 decimal places, 8/4 bytes, truncation rounding risk
decimal/numeric: fixed precision 1-38, default (18,0), 5/9/13/17 bytes
datetime: avoid for new work; 3.33 ms rounding; not ANSI/ISO compliant
datetime2: 0001-9999, 100 ns, 6-8 bytes; datetimeoffset for time zones
nvarchar(n): n is byte-pairs not characters; (max) adds 24-byte sort overhead
uniqueidentifier: 16-byte GUID; NEWSEQUENTIALID only in DEFAULT constraints
NEWSEQUENTIALID privacy warning and post-failover value clustering
engineering_principles: RECOMMENDED against money: 'You can experience rounding errors through truncation ... Avoid using this data type if your money or currency values are used in calculations. Instead, use the decimal data type with at least four decimal places.' RECOMMENDED against datetime: 'Avoid using datetime for new work. Instead, use the time, date, datetime2, and datetimeoffset data types. These types align with the SQL Standard, and are more portable ... datetimeoffset provides time zone support for globally deployed applications.' nvarchar: 'Use nchar when the sizes of the column data entries are consistent. Use nvarchar when the sizes ... vary considerably. Use nvarchar(max) when ... the string length might exceed 4,000 byte-pairs.' GUIDs: NEWSEQUENTIALID 'can be faster than using the NEWID function ... helps to completely fill the data and index pages' but 'If privacy is a concern, don't use this function' and 'clusters of sequential values can develop' after failover or database moves; 'unique across multiple computers only if the source computer has a network card'. MANDATORY: NEWSEQUENTIALID 'can only be used with DEFAULT constraints on table columns of type uniqueidentifier'.
practical_examples: CREATE TABLE myTable (ColumnA UNIQUEIDENTIFIER DEFAULT NEWSEQUENTIALID()); CREATE TABLE dbo.MyTable (MyDecimalColumn DECIMAL(5,2), MyNumericColumn NUMERIC(10,5)); CAST('01/01/2024 23:59:59.999' AS DATETIME) -> '2024-01-02 00:00:00.000' (rounding demo); DECLARE @MyDatetime2 datetime2(7).
why_it_matters: Settles three recurring schema arguments with vendor text: exact decimal (not money) for arithmetic, datetime2/datetimeoffset (not datetime) for new work, and the real cost/benefit of GUID keys. Also clarifies that nvarchar(n) sizes are byte-pairs, which affects column sizing for Unicode data.
authority_rationale: Official T-SQL reference pages maintained by Microsoft with ms.date values; apply to SQL Server, Azure SQL Database/MI, Synapse and Fabric.
notes: Sibling pages fetched: decimal and numeric (ms.date 2026-10-13) https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/t-sql/data-types/decimal-and-numeric-transact-sql; datetime (2026-06-29) https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/t-sql/data-types/datetime-transact-sql; datetime2 (2024-10-25) https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/t-sql/data-types/datetime2-transact-sql; nchar and nvarchar (2024-06-06) https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/t-sql/data-types/nchar-and-nvarchar-transact-sql; uniqueidentifier (2024-09-24) https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/t-sql/data-types/uniqueidentifier-transact-sql; NEWSEQUENTIALID (2025-10-20) https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/t-sql/functions/newsequentialid-transact-sql. SQL Server 2025 adds native json and vector types (What's New page, ms.date 2026-09-28).

title: Temporal tables (system-versioned) and Ledger overview (SQL Server)
organization_author: Microsoft (SQL Server documentation; authors thesqlsith/derekw; ledger page VanMSFT)
core_concepts: PERIOD FOR SYSTEM_TIME with two datetime2 columns (UTC, transaction begin time)
history table with mirrored schema; FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF / FROM..TO / BETWEEN / CONTAINED IN / ALL
primary key required on current table; history table cannot have constraints or PK
no TRUNCATE while SYSTEM_VERSIONING ON; no INSTEAD OF triggers; no FILESTREAM
recommended clustered columnstore on history table; PAGE compression default
ledger: updatable (system-versioned + history) and append-only ledger tables, SHA-256 Merkle tree blockchain, database digests in immutable storage
ledger database cannot be converted back
engineering_principles: MANDATORY: 'A temporal table must have a primary key defined ... The history table can't have a primary key defined'; period columns 'must be defined with a data type of datetime2'; history table 'can't have constraints'; 'TRUNCATE TABLE isn't supported while SYSTEM_VERSIONING is ON'; 'INSTEAD OF triggers aren't permitted'. RECOMMENDED: 'An optimal indexing strategy includes a clustered columnstore index or a B-tree rowstore index on the current table, and a clustered columnstore index on the history table'; be careful with LOB columns ('significant storage costs'). Row-level security predicates, indexes, partitioning and check constraints are NOT propagated to the history table. Ledger (OPTIONAL/CONTEXTUAL): 'Ledger can't prevent such attacks but guarantees that any tampering will be detected when the ledger data is verified'; store digests outside the database 'in tamper-proof storage'.
practical_examples: CREATE TABLE dbo.Employee ([EmployeeID] INT NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY CLUSTERED, [Name] NVARCHAR(100) NOT NULL, ..., [AnnualSalary] DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL, [ValidFrom] DATETIME2 GENERATED ALWAYS AS ROW START, [ValidTo] DATETIME2 GENERATED ALWAYS AS ROW END, PERIOD FOR SYSTEM_TIME (ValidFrom, ValidTo)) WITH (SYSTEM_VERSIONING = ON (HISTORY_TABLE = dbo.EmployeeHistory)); SELECT * FROM Employee FOR SYSTEM_TIME BETWEEN '2021-01-01 00:00:00.0000000' AND '2022-01-01 00:00:00.0000000' WHERE EmployeeID = 1000 ORDER BY ValidFrom;
why_it_matters: Gives schema designers a declarative, engine-managed alternative to hand-built audit/history tables (and SCD Type 2 dimensions), with the exact constraints that must be designed in (PK, datetime2, no history-table constraints). Ledger extends the same structure with cryptographic tamper evidence for regulated data.
authority_rationale: Official vendor documentation; temporal applies to SQL Server 2016+, Azure SQL DB/MI, Fabric SQL database; ledger applies to SQL Server 2022+ and Azure SQL.
notes: Canonical URL resolves to .../tables/temporal/overview. Also read: Temporal table considerations and limitations, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/tables/temporal-table-considerations-and-limitations (ms.date 2026-08-18) and Ledger overview, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/security/ledger/ledger-overview (ms.date 2025-08-07). SQL Server supports only system time (no application/valid-time period), unlike Oracle Temporal Validity.

title: Row-level security (SQL Server) with Dynamic Data Masking, Always Encrypted and Transparent Data Encryption
organization_author: Microsoft (SQL Server documentation; author VanMSFT; AE page Pietervanhove; TDE page adbadram)
core_concepts: RLS filter predicates vs block predicates; inline TVF + CREATE SECURITY POLICY
RLS applies to all users including dbo; side-channel (divide-by-zero) inference
DDM functions default/email/random/partial/datetime; UNMASK granular permission (2022+)
DDM and Data Redaction-style caveat: not protection against ad hoc inference
Always Encrypted deterministic vs randomized; keys never visible to engine; _BIN2 collation required
Always Encrypted unsupported column types and constraints (IDENTITY, computed, default, check, partitioning, DDM)
TDE page-level encryption at rest; DEK/certificate hierarchy; backups encrypted; tempdb encrypted
engineering_principles: RLS RECOMMENDED: 'create a separate schema for the RLS objects'; 'Avoid type conversions', 'Avoid recursion', 'Avoid using excessive table joins in predicate functions'; predicates must not depend on SET DATEFORMAT/LANGUAGE/ANSI_WARNINGS. 'Security policies apply to all users, including dbo users'; indexed views cannot be built on RLS tables; temporal history tables need their own predicate. DDM: 'dynamic data masking shouldn't be used alone to fully secure sensitive data from users running ad hoc queries ... doesn't protect against malicious intent to infer the underlying data'; 'Creating a mask on a column doesn't prevent updates'. Always Encrypted MANDATORY schema constraints: string columns must use _BIN2 collation; not supported on xml/rowversion/sql_variant/hierarchyid/spatial/vector, IDENTITY, ROWGUIDCOL, computed, sparse, partitioning columns, default or check constraints, DDM-masked columns; PK/unique/FK only with deterministic encryption; randomized encryption 'doesn't support searching, grouping, indexing, or joining'. TDE MANDATORY operational rule: 'Backup files for databases that have TDE enabled are also encrypted with the DEK ... Data loss results if the certificates are no longer available'; 'TDE doesn't provide encryption across communication channels'; FILESTREAM not encrypted.
practical_examples: CREATE FUNCTION Security.tvf_securitypredicate(@SalesRep AS nvarchar(50)) RETURNS TABLE WITH SCHEMABINDING AS RETURN SELECT 1 AS tvf_securitypredicate_result WHERE @SalesRep = USER_NAME() OR USER_NAME() = 'Manager'; CREATE SECURITY POLICY SalesFilter ADD FILTER PREDICATE Security.tvf_securitypredicate(SalesRep) ON Sales.Orders WITH (STATE = ON); multi-tenant: WHERE DATABASE_PRINCIPAL_ID() = DATABASE_PRINCIPAL_ID('AppUser') AND CAST(SESSION_CONTEXT(N'UserId') AS int) = @AppUserId with EXEC sp_set_session_context @key=N'UserId', @value=2, @read_only=1. DDM: FirstName VARCHAR(100) MASKED WITH (FUNCTION = 'partial(1, "xxxxx", 1)') NULL; GRANT UNMASK ON Data.Membership(FirstName) TO ServiceAttendant. TDE: CREATE DATABASE ENCRYPTION KEY WITH ALGORITHM = AES_256 ENCRYPTION BY SERVER CERTIFICATE MyServerCert; ALTER DATABASE AdventureWorks2022 SET ENCRYPTION ON;
why_it_matters: Each feature imposes schema-level constraints (dedicated security schema, BIN2 collations, no computed/default columns under Always Encrypted, policy-per-history-table) and each page states its own limits, so a schema design framework can label them 'defense in depth' rather than substitutes for access control.
authority_rationale: Official vendor documentation for SQL Server 2016+/Azure SQL with ms.date values; limitations sections are vendor-authored.
notes: Companion pages fetched: Dynamic data masking https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/security/dynamic-data-masking (ms.date 2025-06-30); Always Encrypted https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/security/encryption/always-encrypted-database-engine (ms.date 2026-01-28); Transparent data encryption https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/security/encryption/transparent-data-encryption (ms.date 2025-09-07). Fabric/Synapse support RLS filter predicates only (no block predicates).

title: SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL (Transact-SQL)
organization_author: Microsoft (SQL Server T-SQL reference; author uc-msft, reviewer wiassaf)
subcategory: Transactions, isolation, locking and row versioning
core_concepts: READ COMMITTED is the SQL Server default
READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT OFF by default on SQL Server, ON by default on Azure SQL Database and Fabric SQL database
SNAPSHOT requires ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION; readers and writers do not block each other
REPEATABLE READ / SERIALIZABLE lower concurrency; range locks
shared locks can escalate to page/table locks
Azure Synapse default READ UNCOMMITTED
SQL Server 2025 optimized locking avoids lock escalation
engineering_principles: 'READ COMMITTED ... This option is the SQL Server default.' 'If READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT is set to OFF (the default on SQL Server), the Database Engine uses shared locks ... If ... ON, the Database Engine uses row versioning to present each statement with a transactionally consistent snapshot ... READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON is the default on Azure SQL Database and SQL database in Microsoft Fabric.' 'The ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION database option must be set to ON before you can start a transaction that uses the SNAPSHOT isolation level.' REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE: 'use this option only when necessary' (RECOMMENDED). 'A transaction always gets an exclusive lock on any data it modifies ... regardless of the isolation level.' Contrast: Oracle 'never escalates locks' and never permits dirty reads; SQL Server offers READ UNCOMMITTED (dirty reads).
practical_examples: SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ; BEGIN TRANSACTION; SELECT * FROM HumanResources.EmployeePayHistory; COMMIT TRANSACTION; database options ALTER DATABASE ... SET READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON / ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION ON; READCOMMITTEDLOCK table hint to force locking under RCSI.
why_it_matters: Schema design interacts with concurrency: hot narrow clustered keys, lock escalation and the choice between locking READ COMMITTED and RCSI determine whether OLTP schemas suffer blocking. Knowing that Azure SQL defaults to RCSI while on-premises SQL Server does not avoids behavioral surprises when migrating a schema.
authority_rationale: Official T-SQL reference from Microsoft, versioned for SQL Server 2017-2025, Azure SQL, Synapse and Fabric.
notes: SQL Server 2025 'Optimized locking' (Reduces blocking and lock memory consumption, and avoids lock escalation) is listed on https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/sql-server/what-s-new-in-sql-server-2025 (ms.date 2026-09-28).

title: Backup overview (SQL Server) and What is an Always On availability group?
organization_author: Microsoft (SQL Server documentation; backup author dnethi; AG author dimitri-furman)
core_concepts: full, differential, transaction log, file/filegroup, partial, copy-only backups
recovery models simple / full / bulk-logged; full model requires log backups
no table-level backups
availability group = set of databases failing over together; 1 primary + up to 8 secondaries
synchronous-commit (no data loss, higher latency; up to 5 sync replicas) vs asynchronous-commit (possible data loss)
secondary replicas are not backups
SQL Server 2025: ZSTD backup compression, immutable blob backup, full/differential backups on secondaries
engineering_principles: 'A backup of SQL Server data is created at the level of a database or one or more of its files or filegroups. Table-level backups cannot be created. In addition to data backups, the full recovery model requires creating backups of the transaction log.' Differential backup 'contains only the data extents that have changed since the differential base'. AG MANDATORY: 'Secondary databases aren't backups. Continue to back up your databases and their transaction logs regularly.' 'Under asynchronous-commit mode, the primary replica commits transactions without waiting ... making some data loss possible'; 'Synchronous-commit mode ensures that once a given secondary database is synchronized ... committed transactions are fully protected. This protection comes at the cost of increased transaction latency.' Secondary databases are seeded with RESTORE WITH NORECOVERY; AG is 'an enterprise-level alternative to database mirroring'. Partitioning tie-in: multiple filegroups allow piecemeal backup/restore of static partitions.
practical_examples: BACKUP ... WITH COPY_ONLY / PARTIAL options required via T-SQL; AG topology: one primary replica, 1-8 secondary replicas on different WSFC nodes; listener with DNS name/VIP for client failover; REQUIRED_SYNCHRONIZED_SECONDARIES_TO_COMMIT; secondaries can take log and copy-only backups (full/differential from 2025).
why_it_matters: Backup/restore capability and HA topology are schema-adjacent decisions (filegroup placement of partitions, TDE certificate backups, recovery model) and the vendor's explicit statement that replicas are not backups is a mandatory design rule shared with Oracle and MongoDB.
authority_rationale: Official Microsoft documentation; AG page ms.date 2026-01-26 and covers SQL Server 2025 TDS 8/TLS 1.3 changes.
notes: AG overview fetched at https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/database-engine/availability-groups/windows/overview-of-always-on-availability-groups-sql-server (ms.date 2026-01-26). Backup overview page is older (2023) but still current for SQL Server 2025 moniker. SQL Server 2025 GA status taken from What's New page linking the 'SQL Server 2025 is now generally available' Tech Community post.

title: Data Integrity (Oracle Database Concepts) with Data Concurrency and Consistency
organization_author: Oracle Corporation (Oracle AI Database Concepts guide)
subcategory: Integrity constraints, keys, constraint states, concurrency model
core_concepts: declarative integrity constraints vs application code (declarative ease, centralized rules, flexible loading)
NOT NULL, unique, primary key, foreign key, check constraints; natural vs surrogate keys
referential actions: no action, DELETE CASCADE, DELETE SET NULL
constraint states ENABLE/DISABLE x VALIDATE/NOVALIDATE; DEFERRABLE; PRECHECK (JSON schema)
rule: foreign keys should be indexed (locking and full-scan avoidance)
multiversion read consistency; read committed default; serializable; read-only
readers never block writers; Oracle never escalates locks; no dirty reads
engineering_principles: RECOMMENDED: 'To enforce data integrity, use integrity constraints or assertions whenever possible.' Advantages: 'no additional programming is required'; 'data entered by all applications must adhere to the same integrity constraints'; constraints can be disabled 'to avoid performance overhead when loading large amounts of data'. Keys: surrogate key 'is a system-generated incrementing identifier ... Typically, a sequence or UUID generates surrogate keys'. FK indexing (RECOMMENDED, effectively mandatory for OLTP concurrency): 'As a rule, foreign keys should be indexed. The only exception is when the matching unique or primary key is never updated or deleted' because it 'Prevents a full table lock on the child table' and 'Removes the need for a full table scan of the child table'. Concurrency: 'Oracle AI Database offers the read committed (default) and serializable isolation levels'; 'never permits a dirty read'; 'A reader never blocks a writer ... A writer never blocks a reader'; 'Oracle AI Database never escalates locks. Lock escalation greatly increases the probability of deadlocks.'
practical_examples: CONSTRAINT emp_email_uk UNIQUE (email); ALTER TABLE employees ADD CONSTRAINT max_emp_sal CHECK (salary < 10001); constraint states ENABLE VALIDATE / ENABLE NOVALIDATE / DISABLE VALIDATE / DISABLE NOVALIDATE; INITIALLY DEFERRED with SET CONSTRAINT; optimistic update pattern UPDATE employees SET email = ?, phone_number = ? WHERE employee_id = ? AND email = ? AND phone_number = ?;
why_it_matters: Oracle's canonical argument for database-enforced integrity over application checks, plus the FK-index rule that is stronger than SQL Server's because unindexed FKs cause child-table locking in Oracle. The MVCC model explains why Oracle's schema advice focuses less on lock avoidance than SQL Server's.
authority_rationale: Official Oracle Concepts guide; the /23/ URL opened resolved to the current Oracle AI Database 26ai Concepts content (paths under /oracle-database/26/cncpt/).
notes: URL requested with /23/ path; content served was Oracle AI Database 26ai (no per-page date). Concurrency chapter fetched at https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/26/cncpt/data-concurrency-and-consistency.html. The Concepts page does NOT prescribe short/immutable primary keys; that guidance is SQL Server-specific. Data Warehousing Guide (MSOM-12) deliberately relaxes constraint enforcement (RELY) for DW.

title: Indexes and Index-Organized Tables (Oracle Database Concepts)
organization_author: Oracle Corporation (Oracle AI Database 26ai Concepts guide)
subcategory: Indexes (B-tree, bitmap, bitmap join, function-based, invisible) and table organization (heap vs IOT)
core_concepts: index is optional and physically independent of table data; DML overhead
when to index: frequently queried + small percentage of rows; FK columns; unique constraints
B-tree standard, best for highly selective and PK indexes
bitmap for low cardinality, read-mostly/DW; not for many OLTP applications (locks many rows)
bitmap join indexes and function-based indexes
invisible indexes for safe index removal testing
heap-organized tables default; index-organized tables require PK, 'the index is the data'
engineering_principles: 'The database must update the index when DML occurs on the indexed data, which creates performance overhead.' Create an index when 'The indexed columns are queried frequently and return a small percentage of the total number of rows' or 'A referential integrity constraint exists on the indexed column'. 'B-tree indexes are the standard index type. They are excellent for highly selective indexes ... and primary key indexes.' Bitmap (CONTEXTUAL DW): 'primarily designed for data warehousing or environments in which queries reference many columns in an ad hoc fashion'; 'Because a key points to many rows, DML on indexed data typically locks all of these rows. For this reason, bitmap indexes are not appropriate for many OLTP applications.' Table organization: 'a heap-organized table inserts rows where they fit' (default); IOT 'useful when related pieces of data must be stored together or data must be physically stored in a specific order ... information retrieval, spatial data, and OLAP applications' and 'a primary key constraint must be defined'. Invisible index: 'especially useful for testing the removal of an index before dropping it.'
practical_examples: CREATE BITMAP INDEX employees_bm_idx ON employees (jobs.job_title) FROM employees, jobs WHERE employees.job_id = jobs.job_id; CREATE INDEX emp_fname_uppercase_idx ON employees ( UPPER(first_name) ); SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers WHERE cust_gender = 'F' AND cust_marital_status IN ('single','divorced') -- bitmap AND example.
why_it_matters: Shows the key structural difference from SQL Server: Oracle tables are heaps by default and clustering (IOT) is the exception, so Oracle PK guidance does not revolve around a clustered key. It also fixes bitmap indexes as a DW-only tool and offers invisible indexes as the safe path for index cleanup (parallel to MongoDB hideIndex).
authority_rationale: Official Oracle Concepts guide for the current release (Oracle AI Database 26ai); URL returned verbatim by search and fetched.
notes: Initially fetched via /23/ path which resolved to this 26ai content. Partitioned-table indexing rules (local vs global) are in MSOM-11.

title: Data Types and Database Object Names and Qualifiers (Oracle SQL Language Reference)
organization_author: Oracle Corporation (Oracle AI Database SQL Language Reference)
subcategory: Data types; identifier rules and naming guidance
core_concepts: NUMBER(p,s): precision 1-38, scale -84..127, 1-22 bytes; specify precision/scale for integrity
BINARY_FLOAT/BINARY_DOUBLE recommended over FLOAT
VARCHAR2 4000/32767 bytes (MAX_STRING_SIZE); never use VARCHAR; CHAR blank-pads
DATE (to seconds, 7 bytes) vs TIMESTAMP(0-9) vs TIMESTAMP WITH [LOCAL] TIME ZONE
BOOLEAN and native binary JSON types (recommended for JSON columns); LONG deprecated -> LOBs
identifiers 128 bytes at COMPATIBLE >= 12.2 (30 bytes below); nonquoted uppercase; reserved words
naming guidance: descriptive pronounceable names, consistent rules, same name for same attribute across tables; avoid quoted identifiers, $ and #, SYS_/ORA_ prefixes
engineering_principles: RECOMMENDED: 'It is good practice to specify the scale and precision of a fixed-point number column for extra integrity checking on input ... If a value exceeds the precision, then Oracle returns an error. If a value exceeds the scale, then Oracle rounds it.' 'Oracle recommends that you use the BINARY_FLOAT and BINARY_DOUBLE data types instead [of FLOAT].' MANDATORY-style: 'Do not use the VARCHAR data type. Use the VARCHAR2 data type instead ... might be redefined in a future release.' 'Do not create tables with LONG columns. Use LOB columns (CLOB, NCLOB, BLOB) instead.' 'Oracle recommends that you use JSON data type for the JSON columns.' TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE 'is useful for preserving local time zone information'; DATE 'does not have fractional seconds or a time zone'. Names: 'names must be from 1 to 128 bytes long' (COMPATIBLE >= 12.2); 'Oracle does not recommend using quoted identifiers for database object names'; 'Oracle strongly discourages you from using $ and # in nonquoted identifiers'; 'Do not use words beginning with SYS_ or ORA_'; 'Use full, descriptive, pronounceable names (or well-known abbreviations)'; 'Use consistent naming rules'; 'Use the same name to describe the same entity or attribute across tables.'
practical_examples: NUMBER(6,1) stores 123.89 as 123.9; NUMBER(3,2) cannot hold 123.89 (error); CREATE TABLE example (id NUMBER, c1 BOOLEAN, c2 BOOL); CREATE TABLE j_purchaseorder (id VARCHAR2(32) NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY, date_loaded TIMESTAMP(6) WITH TIME ZONE, po_document JSON(OBJECT)); valid names: last_name, hr.hire_date, a_very_long_and_valid_name; department_id used identically in employees and departments.
why_it_matters: Supplies Oracle's exact-numeric and timestamp guidance (parallel to SQL Server decimal/datetime2 and MongoDB Decimal128) and is the only one of the three vendors to publish explicit, if brief, naming-convention guidance beyond identifier rules.
authority_rationale: Official Oracle SQL Language Reference; /23/ URLs opened resolved to Oracle AI Database 26ai content.
notes: Companion page fetched: Database Object Names and Qualifiers, https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/23/sqlrf/Database-Object-Names-and-Qualifiers.html (also resolved to 26ai). The Data Types page did not state the release in which BOOLEAN was introduced. Data Types page is ~125k chars; the final ~20% (mostly rowid/ANSI type mappings) was not read.

title: Partitioning Concepts (Oracle VLDB and Partitioning Guide)
organization_author: Oracle Corporation (Oracle AI Database VLDB and Partitioning Guide 26ai, G43505-02 January 2026)
core_concepts: partitioning transparent to applications; benefits: performance (pruning), manageability (rolling window), availability
strategies: range, hash, list, composite, interval, reference, virtual-column, partition-by-expression
up to one million partitions; tables > 2 GB are always candidates
local vs global indexes decision order; bitmap indexes must be local
partition pruning 'several orders of magnitude'; partition-wise joins
hybrid partitioned tables restrictions (RELY DISABLE constraints only)
engineering_principles: 'From the perspective of the application, a partitioned table is identical to a nonpartitioned table.' RECOMMENDED when to partition: 'Tables that are greater than 2 GB. These tables should always be considered as candidates for partitioning'; historical tables where only the newest partition is updatable; tables spread across storage tiers. Index decision rules in order: (1) partitioning column is a subset of index keys -> local; (2) unique index not containing the partitioning key -> global; (3) manageability priority -> local; (4) 'For OLTP with quick response times, use global. For DSS focused on throughput, use local.' 'Bitmap indexes must be local.' 'Partition pruning can often improve query performance by several orders of magnitude.' Partition-wise joins apply 'when two tables are being joined and both tables are partitioned on the join key'. MANDATORY: 'All partitions of a partitioned object must reside in tablespaces of the same block size'; LONG/LONG RAW tables cannot be partitioned.
practical_examples: CREATE TABLE sales_orders (order_id NUMBER, base_total NUMBER, tax_amount NUMBER) PARTITION BY HASH (base_total + tax_amount) PARTITIONS 8; range partitions with VALUES LESS THAN and MAXVALUE; interval partitioning auto-creates partitions; weekly-partitioned Orders table: a one-week query touches 1 of 104 partitions ('could potentially execute 100 times faster'); ORA_PARTITION_VALIDATION(rowid).
why_it_matters: Oracle is more bullish than SQL Server on partitioning for query performance (SQL Server: 'rarely improves performance in OLTP systems'); the guide's size threshold (2 GB) and local/global index rules are concrete design inputs for large-table schemas and conflict with SQL Server's 15,000-partition cap (Oracle allows a million).
authority_rationale: Official Oracle guide; /23/ URL resolved to the 26ai VLDB and Partitioning Guide whose PDF edition is dated January 2026.
notes: DW-specific partitioning recommendations (composite range-hash, power-of-2 hash partitions >= 16 MB) are in the Data Warehousing Guide (MSOM-12).

title: Data Warehousing Logical Design, Data Warehousing Optimizations and Techniques, and Basic Materialized Views (Oracle Data Warehousing Guide)
organization_author: Oracle Corporation (Oracle AI Database Data Warehousing Guide 26ai, G43670-01 October 2025)
subcategory: Star/3NF schema design, bitmap indexes, star transformation, RELY constraints, DW partitioning, materialized views
core_concepts: 3NF vs star vs snowflake definitions and trade-offs; 3NF foundation layer + star access layer
fact table composite key of dimension PKs; surrogate integer keys recommended for dimensions
FK/referential constraints should be non-enforced (RELY) in DW
grain, conformed dimensions, conformed facts, SCD Type 2 most common
bitmap indexes: >= 100 rows per distinct value; majority of DW indexes should be bitmap; B-tree only for (near-)unique
star transformation prerequisites: bitmap index on every fact FK, STAR_TRANSFORMATION_ENABLED=TRUE
composite range-hash partitioning; power-of-2 hash partitions >= 16 MB; local indexes more common
materialized views with query rewrite; MV logs for fast refresh; COUNT(*) required for aggregates
engineering_principles: '3NF databases use very many tables and this requires complex queries with many joins'; 'The star schema accepts data redundancy (denormalization) in its dimension tables for the sake of easy user understanding and better data retrieval performance'; snowflake 'requires more foreign key joins ... reduced query performance'. 'the modern approach to data warehousing does not pit star schemas and 3NF against each other ... a foundation layer of 3NF ... and star schemas as a central part of an access and performance optimization layer.' RECOMMENDED: 'Surrogate or artificial keys, usually sequential integers, are recommended for dimension tables'; 'Whenever possible, foreign keys and referential integrity constraints should be defined as non-enforced conditions, since it enables better query optimization and cardinality estimates' (conflicts with the OLTP rule in MSOM-08 - context dependent). Indexes: 'Bitmap indexes are primarily intended for data warehousing applications where users query the data rather than update it. They are not suitable for OLTP'; candidate when 'There are 100 or more rows for each distinct value'; 'The majority of indexes in a data warehouse should be bitmap indexes'; 'usually best to use single-column bitmap indexes'. Star transformation: 'A bitmap index should be built on each of the foreign key columns of the fact table'; STAR_TRANSFORMATION_ENABLED 'is set to FALSE by default'. Constraints: 'Creating a RELY constraint is inexpensive and does not impose any overhead during DML or load.' Partitioning: 'The larger tables should be partitioned using composite partitioning (range-hash or list-hash)'; hash partition count 'a power of 2'; 'Each hash partition should be at least 16MB'. MVs: 'create materialized views that satisfy the largest number of queries'; 'Materialized view logs are required if you want to use fast refresh'.
practical_examples: ALTER TABLE sales ADD CONSTRAINT sales_time_fk FOREIGN KEY (time_id) REFERENCES times (time_id) RELY DISABLE NOVALIDATE; ALTER TABLE sales ADD CONSTRAINT sales_uk UNIQUE (prod_id, cust_id, promo_id, channel_id, time_id) DISABLE VALIDATE; CREATE BITMAP INDEX sales_cust_gender_bjix ON sales(customers.cust_gender) FROM sales, customers WHERE sales.cust_id = customers.cust_id LOCAL NOLOGGING COMPUTE STATISTICS; CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW LOG ON sales WITH SEQUENCE, ROWID (prod_id, cust_id, time_id, channel_id, promo_id, quantity_sold, amount_sold) INCLUDING NEW VALUES; CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW product_sales_mv BUILD IMMEDIATE REFRESH FAST ENABLE QUERY REWRITE AS SELECT p.prod_name, SUM(s.amount_sold) AS dollar_sales, COUNT(*) AS cnt, COUNT(s.amount_sold) AS cnt_amt FROM sales s JOIN products p ON (s.prod_id = p.prod_id) GROUP BY p.prod_name; ALTER TABLE SALES DROP PARTITION Sales_Q4_2009;
why_it_matters: The clearest official statement that warehouse schema rules invert OLTP rules: denormalized star dimensions with integer surrogate keys, bitmap rather than B-tree indexes, RELY rather than enforced constraints, and pre-aggregated materialized views. Essential for labeling principles as OLTP-vs-DW contextual rather than universal.
authority_rationale: Official Oracle Data Warehousing Guide for the current release (26ai, PDF edition October 2025); three chapters fetched.
notes: Chapters fetched: Logical Design (this URL); Optimizations and Techniques https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/26/dwhsg/data-warehouse-optimizations-techniques.html; Basic Materialized Views https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/26/dwhsg/basic-materialized-views.html. Internal inconsistency flagged: the Optimizations page also says 'Indexes are more beneficial for high cardinality columns' (generic B-tree statement) alongside its low-cardinality bitmap guidance. Oracle Licensing docs (per search snippet, not fetched) list bitmap indexes as unavailable on Free/SE2 editions.

title: About Oracle Virtual Private Database (Security Guide) with Transparent Data Encryption, Data Redaction and Unified Auditing introductions
organization_author: Oracle Corporation (Oracle AI Database Security Guide 26ai G43025-06 July 2026; TDE Guide G43027-06; Data Redaction Guide G43026-03)
subcategory: Security features: row/column access control, encryption at rest, redaction, auditing
core_concepts: VPD adds a dynamic WHERE clause to SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/INDEX/DELETE on tables, views, synonyms
policy types static / context-sensitive / dynamic; DBMS_RLS; SYS_CONTEXT application context
VPD does not protect against SYS or DBA-role users; RAS recommended for new projects
TDE column vs tablespace encryption; master key in keystore (wallet, Oracle Key Vault, OCI Vault); AES256 default in 26ai; BFILE not encrypted
Data Redaction: full/partial/regex/random/nullify/none at query time; PDB-level policies; inference via WHERE clause possible
Unified auditing enabled by default; traditional auditing desupported in 26ai; AUDSYS.AUD$UNIFIED insert-only; ORA_SECURECONFIG and ORA_LOGIN_LOGOUT
engineering_principles: VPD: 'Essentially, Oracle Virtual Private Database adds a dynamic WHERE clause to a SQL statement that is issued against the table, view, or synonym'; benefits 'Security ... Simplicity ... Flexibility'; 'Oracle Database does not protect tables and views that have VPD policies against the SYS user and against users who have an out-of-the-box database administrator role'; 'Oracle recommends that you use RAS for new projects that require row and column level access controls' (RECOMMENDED). TDE: 'TDE enables you to encrypt sensitive data that you store in tables and tablespaces. It also enables you to encrypt database backups'; tablespace encryption 'useful if your tables contain sensitive data in multiple columns ... allows index range scans'; column encryption for specific sensitive columns ('choose the NO SALT parameter' for indexed columns); 'The default encryption algorithm ... is AES256'; 3DES168 'should not be used in new deployments'. Redaction caveats (vendor's own): 'not designed to prevent data exposure to database users who run ad hoc queries directly against the database'; 'the WHERE clause can be used in an iterative fashion to infer the actual data'; 'redacted data can be written back to this database'. Auditing: 'unified auditing is enabled by default'; 'Traditional auditing is desupported in Oracle AI Database 26ai'; best practices: use predefined policies, 'collect the amount of information that you need to meet compliance requirements', archive/purge with DBMS_AUDIT_MGMT, separate tablespace, separate AUDIT_ADMIN and AUDIT_VIEWER.
practical_examples: SELECT * FROM OE.ORDERS; -- rewritten by VPD to SELECT * FROM OE.ORDERS WHERE SALES_REP_ID = 159; SELECT * FROM orders_tab WHERE custno = SYS_CONTEXT('order_entry','cust_num'); GRANT ADMINISTER ROW LEVEL SECURITY POLICY ON SCHEMA schema TO grantee; SELECT KEYSTORE_MODE, CON_ID FROM V$ENCRYPTION_WALLET; partial redaction example output ***-**-4320; CREATE AUDIT POLICY ... / AUDIT POLICY ...; SELECT ... FROM unified_audit_trail.
why_it_matters: Mirrors the SQL Server security stack (RLS/TDE/DDM/Audit) with Oracle-specific design consequences: VPD is superseded by RAS for new work, TDE tablespace vs column choice affects indexing, redaction is explicitly not an access-control boundary, and auditing is on by default so audit trail storage must be planned.
authority_rationale: Official Oracle Security, TDE and Data Redaction guides for the current 26ai release (PDF editions July 2026); detailed redaction types/caveats were read from the 19c Advanced Security Guide page, whose intro text matches the 26ai page.
notes: Also fetched: TDE intro 26ai https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/26/dbtde/introduction-to-transparent-data-encryption.html and 19c https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/19/asoag/introduction-to-transparent-data-encryption.html; Data Redaction intro 26ai https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/26/dbred/introduction-to-oracle-data-redaction.html and 19c https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/19/asoag/introduction-to-oracle-data-redaction.html; Introduction to Auditing 26ai https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/26/dbseg/introduction-to-auditing.html. Note: the auditing page says traditional auditing is desupported in 26ai (not 23ai). Several guessed 26/23/19 slugs returned 404 before the correct ones were found via search.

title: Using Oracle Flashback Technology and Design Basics (Temporal Validity), with Multitenant and Backup/Recovery introductions (Oracle Database Development Guide and related guides)
organization_author: Oracle Corporation (Oracle AI Database Database Development Guide 26ai G43974-07 July 2026; Multitenant Administrator's Guide; Backup and Recovery User's Guide)
subcategory: History/temporal features, multitenant architecture, backup and recovery
core_concepts: Flashback Query AS OF, Version Query VERSIONS BETWEEN, Transaction Query/Backout, Flashback Table/Drop/Database
undo-based flashback not guaranteed (UNDO_RETENTION); Flashback Data Archive (Flashback Time Travel) for long-term history
Temporal Validity: PERIOD FOR valid-time dimension, AS OF PERIOD FOR, VERSIONS PERIOD FOR, DBMS_FLASHBACK_ARCHIVE.ENABLE_AT_VALID_TIME
OLTP fully normalized vs DW denormalized/star (Design Basics)
multitenant CDB/PDB only supported architecture since 21c; CDB$ROOT, PDB$SEED, application containers; C## common users
RMAN preferred; physical backups foundation, logical (Data Pump) insufficient alone; incremental backups; Flashback Database needs fast recovery area
engineering_principles: 'Oracle Flashback Technology is a group of Oracle Database features that let you view past states of database objects or to return database objects to a previous state without using point-in-time media recovery.' MANDATORY caveat: 'Setting UNDO_RETENTION does not guarantee that unexpired undo data is not discarded' -> use Flashback Archive for durable history; Flashback Archive cannot be enabled on LONG, nested table, temporary, external tables or MVs; 'Adding or enabling a constraint fails with ORA-55610'; wait '20 seconds before inserting data and ... up to 5 minutes before using Flashback Query'; archive degrades 'when its space usage exceeds 90%'. Temporal Validity: 'lets you associate one or more valid time dimensions with a table and have data be visible depending on its time-based validity'. Design Basics: 'OLTP systems use fully normalized schemas, while data warehouses use denormalized or star schemas.' Multitenant MANDATORY: 'Starting in Oracle Database 21c, a multitenant container database is the only supported architecture'; 'A PDB is a portable collection of schemas ... that appears to an application as a separate database'; common user names must begin with 'c##'. Backup: 'RMAN is the preferred solution'; 'Physical backups are the foundation of any sound backup and recovery strategy. Logical backups ... are not sufficient protection against data loss without physical backups.'
practical_examples: CREATE FLASHBACK ARCHIVE DEFAULT fla1 TABLESPACE tbs1 QUOTA 10G RETENTION 1 YEAR; CREATE TABLE employee (...) FLASHBACK ARCHIVE fla1; ALTER TABLE employee FLASHBACK ARCHIVE fla1; SELECT * FROM employee AS OF TIMESTAMP (SYSTIMESTAMP - INTERVAL '2' DAY); CREATE TABLE my_emp(empno NUMBER, last_name VARCHAR2(30), start_time TIMESTAMP, end_time TIMESTAMP, PERIOD FOR user_valid_time (start_time, end_time)); SELECT * FROM my_emp AS OF PERIOD FOR user_valid_time TO_TIMESTAMP('01-Jun-10'); ALTER TABLE my_emp ADD PERIOD FOR user_valid_time; CREATE PLUGGABLE DATABASE hrpdb ADMIN USER dba1 IDENTIFIED BY password; CREATE PLUGGABLE DATABASE salespdb FROM hrpdb; RMAN BACKUP INCREMENTAL; FLASHBACK DATABASE.
why_it_matters: Oracle is the only one of the three engines whose docs provide both system-time history (Flashback Archive) and application/valid-time periods (PERIOD FOR) declaratively, which matters for SCD and bitemporal designs; the mandatory CDB/PDB architecture and the physical-backup rule are structural constraints on any Oracle schema deployment.
authority_rationale: Official Oracle guides for the current 26ai release; pages fetched directly from docs.oracle.com /26/ paths.
notes: Also fetched: Design Basics (Temporal Validity Support) https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/26/adfns/design_basics.html; Introduction to Multitenant Administration https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/26/multi/introduction-to-the-multitenant-architecture.html; Introduction to Backup and Recovery https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/26/bradv/introduction-backup-recovery.html. The backup intro page does not cover ARCHIVELOG mode or Data Guard; the multitenant page does not state a max PDB count.

title: Data Modeling in MongoDB (with Designing Your Schema, Best Practices for Data Modeling, Schema Design Patterns and Schema Design Anti-Patterns)
subcategory: Data modeling principles, embedding vs referencing, design patterns, anti-patterns
core_concepts: flexible/polymorphic schema; schema validation optional
core principle: data accessed together should be stored together
four-step process: identify workload, map relationships, apply design patterns, create indexes
embed vs reference decision criteria; data duplication trade-offs; single-document atomicity
patterns: computed values, group data (bucket/outlier), polymorphic, document/schema versioning, archive, single collection; tree structures
anti-patterns: unbounded arrays, too many collections, unnecessary indexes, bloated documents, too many $lookup
16 MB document limit as the hard ceiling on embedding
engineering_principles: RECOMMENDED (core): 'A core principle of data modeling in MongoDB is that data that's accessed together should be stored together. You should structure your data model based on your application's data access patterns.' Embed when 'You have a has-a or contains relationship', 'Your application queries pieces of information together', 'data that's often updated together'; reference when 'The child side of the relationship has high cardinality', 'Your embedded data grows without bounds', 'Your data is written at different times in a write-heavy workload', 'your data can exist by itself without a parent'. 'Duplicating data can remove the need to perform joins ... However, frequently updating duplicate data can cause heavy workloads.' MANDATORY semantics: 'a write operation is atomic on the level of a single document'; 'the availability of distributed transactions should not be a replacement for effective schema design.' Anti-patterns: 'if you do not limit the number of elements in an array, your documents might exceed the 16MB BSON document size limit. An unbounded array can strain application resources and decrease index performance' -> subset pattern ('best for ... data that is not frequently updated') or referencing ('best for ... large or frequently updated datasets'); bloated documents: 'if documents are too large, the working set might not fit into RAM'; unnecessary indexes: 'Creating indexes for every field in a collection can lead to bloated collections and negatively impact write performance.' Bucket: 'Time series collections apply the bucket pattern automatically, and are suitable for most applications that involve bucketing time series data.' Versioning: 'adds a schemaVersion field to tell the application how it should query each document.'
practical_examples: Book/reviews: unbounded reviews array -> subset (3 embedded reviews + reviews collection) or references (reviews: ['review1','review2']) joined with db.books.aggregate([{ $lookup: { from: 'reviews', localField: 'reviews', foreignField: 'review_id', as: 'reviewDetails' } }]); bloated document split into mainBookInfo and additionalBookDetails with $lookup + $mergeObjects + $replaceRoot; bucket pattern _id '123_1698349623', count field, db.trades.updateOne({ _id: /^123_/, count: { $lt: 10 } }, { $push: { history: {...} }, $inc: { count: 1 }, $setOnInsert: { _id: '123_1698939791', customerId: 123 } }, { upsert: true }); db.courses.aggregate([{ $indexStats: {} }]) then db.courses.hideIndex('building_1') before db.courses.dropIndexes([...]); tree patterns: parent references, child references, array of ancestors, materialized paths, nested sets.
why_it_matters: This is the official document-model counter-doctrine to relational normalization: co-locate and duplicate by access pattern, but within explicit bounds (16 MB, working set in RAM, bounded arrays) and with named anti-patterns. A framework must present embedding as a bounded default, not an absolute, and note the direct conflict with Oracle's 3NF-for-OLTP statement.
authority_rationale: Official MongoDB Database Manual (version selector 9.0 Current); multiple sub-pages fetched directly.
notes: Pages fetched: Data Modeling (this URL); Designing Your Schema https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/data-modeling/schema-design-process/; Best Practices (served when requesting /data-modeling/concepts/embedding-vs-references/); Schema Design Patterns https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/data-modeling/design-patterns/; Bucket Pattern https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/data-modeling/design-patterns/group-data/bucket-pattern/; Document and Schema Versioning https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/data-modeling/design-patterns/data-versioning/; Model Tree Structures https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/applications/data-models-tree-structures/; Anti-Patterns https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/data-modeling/design-antipatterns/ plus unbounded-arrays, bloated-documents and unnecessary-indexes sub-pages. The current manual's pattern page does not list attribute, extended reference, approximation or preallocation patterns (older blog taxonomy); no per-page dates (footer © 2026).

title: Schema Validation (with Specify JSON Schema Validation, Specify Validation Level, Documents, MongoDB Limits and Thresholds, Release Notes for MongoDB 9.0)
subcategory: Integrity ($jsonSchema validation), document structure, field naming, hard limits, version currency
core_concepts: schema validation for established applications; rejects invalid inserts/updates by default
$jsonSchema (JSON Schema draft 4): required, bsonType, minimum/maximum, title/description
validationLevel strict (default) / moderate / constraint (new in 9.0, cannot be bypassed)
validationAction error / errorAndLog (warn via separate page)
document = BSON field/value pairs; _id reserved, unique, immutable, not array/regex; ObjectId default
field names: no null character; 5.0 relaxed $ and .; unique within document; field order significant
limits: 16 MiB document, 100 nesting levels, 64 indexes/collection, 32 fields/compound index, 255-byte namespace (235 sharded), 60 s transaction default
MongoDB 9.0.0 released Sept 28, 2026
engineering_principles: 'MongoDB uses a flexible schema model ... After you establish an application schema, use schema validation to prevent unintended schema changes and data type errors.' 'Schema validation is most useful for an established application with a defined data structure.' 'By default, MongoDB rejects any insert or update operation that would produce an invalid document.' Levels: strict 'applies the same validation rules to all document inserts and updates'; moderate exempts existing non-conforming documents; constraint (9.0) 'guarantees that every document in the collection satisfies the rules ... You cannot bypass document validation' and requires validationAction error or errorAndLog. MANDATORY limits: 'The maximum BSON document size is 16 mebibytes'; 'no more than 100 levels of nesting'; 'The field name _id is reserved for use as a primary key; its value must be unique in the collection, is immutable, and may be of any type other than an array or regex'; 'Field names cannot contain the null character'; 'Each field name must be unique within the document'; 'A single collection can have no more than 64 indexes'; 'no more than 32 fields in a compound index'. Cannot validate admin/local/config or system collections.
practical_examples: db.createCollection('students', { validator: { $jsonSchema: { bsonType: 'object', title: 'Student Object Validation', required: ['address','major','name','year'], properties: { name: { bsonType: 'string', description: "'name' must be a string and is required" }, year: { bsonType: 'int', minimum: 2017, maximum: 3017 }, gpa: { bsonType: ['double'] } } } } }); db.runCommand({ collMod: 'movies', validator: {...}, validationLevel: 'moderate' }); db.runCommand({ collMod: 'movies', prepareConstraintValidationLevel: true }); db.runCommand({ collMod: 'movies', validationLevel: 'constraint', validationAction: 'error' }); example document { _id: ObjectId(...), name: { first: 'Alan', last: 'Turing' }, contribs: [...], views: Long(1250000) }.
why_it_matters: Defines how integrity is (optionally) enforced in a document database and the 9.0 'constraint' level that makes schema rules as binding as relational constraints; the limits page supplies the hard numbers (16 MiB, 64 indexes, 100 levels) that bound every MongoDB schema decision and the naming rules that replace relational identifier rules.
authority_rationale: Official MongoDB Database Manual pages (9.0 Current) and official 9.0 release notes; all fetched directly.
notes: Pages fetched: Specify JSON Schema Validation https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/schema-validation/specify-json-schema/; Specify Validation Level https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/schema-validation/specify-validation-level/; Documents https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/document/; Limits and Thresholds https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/limits/; Release Notes 9.0 https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/release-notes/9.0/ (9.0.0 released Sept 28, 2026; server now validates all ingested BSON by default). The 'warn' validationAction is on a separate page not fetched.

title: The ESR (Equality, Sort, Range) Guideline and Indexing Strategies (MongoDB)
core_concepts: compound index key order: Equality first, then Sort, then Range (ESR); ERS when range is very selective
equality fields keep remaining keys sorted; sort fields before range avoid in-memory sorts
$ne, $nin, $regex are range operators; $in equality under 201 elements with sort, range at 201+
map application queries before indexing; indexes have a write/storage cost; drop unused indexes
MongoDB generally uses one index per query (except $or)
engineering_principles: 'In most cases, applying the ESR (Equality, Sort, Range) Guideline to arrange the index keys creates a more efficient compound index.' 'Ensure that equality fields always come first. Placing equality fields first keeps the remaining index fields in sorted order.' 'If avoiding in-memory sorts is critical, place sort fields before range fields (ESR)'; 'If your range predicate in the query is very selective, then put it before sort fields (ERS)'. 'To improve query efficiency, limit the range bounds and use equality matches to reduce the number of documents to scan.' Strategy (RECOMMENDED): 'Before building indexes, map out your application's queries and the fields they access. Indexes have a performance cost, but are worth it for frequent queries on large data sets'; 'Drop indexes that are no longer used'; 'MongoDB only uses one index to fulfill most queries. However, each clause of an $or query may use a different index.' Caveat: 'The $in behavior change at 201 array elements is not guaranteed to stay the same for all MongoDB versions.'
practical_examples: db.movies.find({ directors: 'David Lynch', runtime: { $lt: 130 } }, { title: 1, year: 1, runtime: 1 }).sort({ year: 1 }) -> optimal index { directors: 1, year: 1, runtime: 1 } (directors = equality, year = sort, runtime = range).
why_it_matters: The ESR rule is MongoDB's equivalent of SQL Server's 'SARGable key columns first, cover the rest' and Oracle's selectivity guidance; it is the one index-ordering heuristic stated as a named rule by a vendor and transfers conceptually to composite B-tree indexes in relational engines.
authority_rationale: Official MongoDB Database Manual (9.0 Current), Indexes > Strategies section.
notes: Indexing Strategies overview fetched at https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/applications/indexes/. Covered-query, selectivity and RAM-fit details live on sub-pages not fetched.

title: Transactions (MongoDB) with Production Considerations, Choose a Shard Key, Model Monetary Data and Backup Methods for a Self-Managed Deployment
subcategory: Transactions and their limits, sharding/shard key selection, monetary data types, backup
core_concepts: multi-document ACID transactions on replica sets/sharded clusters; not on standalone
single-document atomicity + embedding reduce the need for transactions; transactions not a substitute for schema design
60-second default lifetime; no 16 MB total limit but each oplog entry <= 16 MB; 5 ms lock wait; write conflicts abort; one open transaction per session; 9.0 cap on concurrent transactions (10000)
read concern snapshot + w:majority for cross-shard consistency; w:1 can roll back on failover
shard key: high cardinality, low frequency skew, avoid monotonic (or use hashed); choose key covering common queries; reshardCollection since 5.0; _id immutable
monetary data: Decimal128 preferred; double unsuitable; scale-factor long and string alternatives
backup: Cloud/Ops Manager (PITR), filesystem snapshots (journal same volume; sharded clusters need balancer off), mongodump for small deployments
engineering_principles: 'The MongoDB document model supports embedding related data within a single document, which reduces the need for multi-document transactions'; 'for many scenarios, modeling your data appropriately will minimize the need for distributed transactions'; 'a distributed transaction incurs a greater performance cost over single document writes, and the availability of distributed transactions should not be a replacement for effective schema design.' MANDATORY limits: 'MongoDB standalone deployments do not support transactions'; 'a transaction must have a runtime of less than one minute' (transactionLifetimeLimitSeconds default 60); 'each oplog entry still must be within the BSON document size limit of 16MB'; 'transactions wait up to 5 milliseconds to acquire locks'; 'You can have at most one open transaction at a time for a session'; cannot write to capped or system.* collections. Shard key (RECOMMENDED): 'Where possible, choose a shard key with high cardinality'; 'A shard key on a value that increases or decreases monotonically is more likely to distribute inserts to a single chunk ... consider using Hashed Sharding'; 'When the queries do not contain the shard key, the queries are broadcast to all shards'. Money: 'binary-based floating-point arithmetic ... is unable to represent exact decimal fractions ... unsuitable for monetary arithmetic'; 'Using the decimal type for modeling monetary data is preferred over the Scale Factor method.' Backup: mongodump/mongorestore are 'tools for backing up and restoring small MongoDB deployments'; snapshots require 'journaling enabled and the journal must reside on the same logical volume'; only Cloud/Ops Manager 'offers point-in-time recovery' and guaranteed sharded-cluster consistency.
practical_examples: db.gasprices.insertOne({ date: ISODate(), price: Decimal128('2.099'), station: 'Quikstop', grade: 'regular' }); migration db.clothes.updateMany({ price: { $type: 'long' } }, { $mul: { price: Decimal128('0.01') } }); transaction read/write concern: readConcern 'snapshot' with writeConcern { w: 'majority' }; reshardCollection / refineCollectionShardKey commands; backup comparison table: Cloud/Ops Manager RPO/RTO low, PITR yes; snapshots and mongodump PITR no, require write lock on sharded clusters.
why_it_matters: Encodes the document-model position that schema design (embedding) comes before transactions, with the hard transaction limits that make long multi-document units of work impractical; shard key rules are MongoDB's analogue of partitioning-key design; Decimal128 completes the cross-vendor 'exact decimal for money' rule; and the backup page makes the 'dump tools are not enough' point parallel to Oracle and SQL Server.
authority_rationale: Official MongoDB Database Manual pages (9.0 Current), all fetched directly; limits cross-checked against the Limits and Thresholds page.
notes: Pages fetched: Production Considerations https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/transactions-production-consideration/; Choose a Shard Key https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/sharding-choose-a-shard-key/; Model Monetary Data https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/model-monetary-data/; Backup Methods https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/backups/.
